body.en: A triple integral \( \iiint_E f\,dV \) extends the last chapter's double integral to a solid region \( E \) in space — for \( f=1 \), it computes \( E \)'s volume directly. The mechanics are identical to Chapter 4's: reduce to iterated single-variable integrals via Fubini's theorem. The one genuinely new skill is choosing the right coordinate system, since many solids (cylinders, cones, spheres) are far easier to describe in cylindrical or spherical coordinates than in \( x,y,z \).

label.en: ● Definition 5.1 — Triple integral over a box

body.en: For \( f \) continuous on the box \( B=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[p,q] \), partition \( B \) into small boxes of volume \( \Delta V=\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z \) and sum \( f \) at sample points, exactly as in Chapter 4, Definition 4.1: \[ \iiint_B f\,dV=\lim_{\ell,m,n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(x_i^*,y_j^*,z_k^*)\,\Delta V. \] By the same factoring argument as Chapter 4's Theorem 4.1 (Fubini), applied one variable at a time, this equals the iterated integral \( \int_a^b\!\int_c^d\!\int_p^q f\,dz\,dy\,dx \) — in any of the six possible orders, for continuous \( f \) — and for a general (non-box) solid \( E \), the bounds on the inner integrals become functions of the outer variables, just as they did for plane regions in Chapter 4.

label.en: Worked example 5.A — A triple integral over a solid region

body.en:
Compute \( \displaystyle\iiint_E z\,dV \) where \( E \) is bounded below by \( z=0 \), above by \( z=4-x^2-y^2 \), over the disk \( x^2+y^2\le4 \).

Integrating \( z \) first (from \( 0 \) to the paraboloid), then over the disk in polar coordinates: \[ \iiint_E z\,dV=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^{4-r^2}z\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^2\Big[\frac{z^2}{2}\Big]_0^{4-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta. \]

\[ =\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^2\frac{(4-r^2)^2}{2}r\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\int_0^2\frac{r(16-8r^2+r^4)}{2}dr=\pi\int_0^2(16r-8r^3+r^5)\,dr. \]

\[ =\pi\Big[8r^2-2r^4+\frac{r^6}{6}\Big]_0^2=\pi\Big(32-32+\frac{64}{6}\Big)=\frac{32\pi}{3}. \]

Cylindrical coordinates keep \( z \) and switch \( x,y \) to polar: \( x=r\cos\theta \), \( y=r\sin\theta \), \( z=z \). By exactly the argument in Chapter 4's polar-coordinates note (a small cylindrical "box" spanning \( \Delta r,\Delta\theta,\Delta z \) has cross-sectional area \( \approx r\,\Delta r\,\Delta\theta \)), \[ dV=r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta. \] Use cylindrical coordinates whenever a solid has circular symmetry about an axis (cylinders, cones, paraboloids of revolution).

label.en: Worked example 5.B — Volume of a cone via cylindrical coordinates

body.en:
Find the volume of the cone \( z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \) below \( z=3 \).

In cylindrical coordinates the cone is \( z=r \), so the solid is \( r\le z\le3 \), \( 0\le r\le3 \), \( 0\le\theta\le2\pi \): \[ V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^3\!\!\int_r^3 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^3 r(3-r)\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\Big[\frac{3r^2}{2}-\frac{r^3}{3}\Big]_0^3=2\pi(13.5-9)=9\pi. \]

(Check against the elementary cone-volume formula \( \frac13\pi R^2h=\frac13\pi(3^2)(3)=9\pi \). ✓)

Spherical coordinates locate a point by distance from the origin \( \rho\ge0 \), the angle \( \varphi\in[0,\pi] \) down from the positive \( z \)-axis, and the usual \( \theta \) around it: \[ x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\quad y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\quad z=\rho\cos\varphi. \] A small spherical "box" spanning \( \Delta\rho,\Delta\varphi,\Delta\theta \) has one side of length \( \Delta\rho \) (radial), one of length \( \approx\rho\,\Delta\varphi \) (along a meridian, at radius \( \rho \)), and one of length \( \approx\rho\sin\varphi\,\Delta\theta \) (along a circle of latitude, whose radius is \( \rho\sin\varphi \), not \( \rho \) — the same shrinking-toward-the-poles effect a globe's lines of longitude show). Multiplying the three side lengths: \[ dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta. \] Use spherical coordinates whenever a solid has symmetry about a point (balls, spherical shells, cones through the origin).

label.en: Worked example 5.C — Volume of a ball via spherical coordinates

body.en:
Find the volume of the ball \( x^2+y^2+z^2\le R^2 \).

The ball is \( 0\le\rho\le R \), \( 0\le\varphi\le\pi \), \( 0\le\theta\le2\pi \) — all independent, so the integral separates completely: \[ V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^{\pi}\!\!\int_0^{R}\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta=\Big(\int_0^{2\pi}\!d\theta\Big)\Big(\int_0^{\pi}\!\sin\varphi\,d\varphi\Big)\Big(\int_0^{R}\!\rho^2\,d\rho\Big). \]

\[ =(2\pi)\big[-\cos\varphi\big]_0^\pi\Big(\frac{R^3}{3}\Big)=(2\pi)(2)\Big(\frac{R^3}{3}\Big)=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \] — the familiar volume-of-a-sphere formula, derived rather than quoted.

Find the volume of the solid bounded above by the sphere \( \rho=2 \) and below by the cone \( \varphi=\pi/4 \) (an "ice-cream-cone" shaped region).

Show solution

The region is \( 0\le\rho\le2 \), \( 0\le\varphi\le\pi/4 \), \( 0\le\theta\le2\pi \): \[ V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^{\pi/4}\!\!\int_0^{2}\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta=(2\pi)\big[-\cos\varphi\big]_0^{\pi/4}\Big(\frac{8}{3}\Big). \]

\( -\cos(\pi/4)+\cos(0)=1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2} \), so \[ V=(2\pi)\Big(1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\Big)\Big(\frac83\Big)=\frac{16\pi}{3}\Big(1-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\Big)\approx4.80. \]

Set up (do not evaluate) \( \iiint_E xyz\,dV \) for \( E \) the box \( [0,1]\times[0,2]\times[0,3] \).

Solution: A box needs no coordinate change and every bound is constant:

\[ \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^3 xyz\,dz\,dy\,dx. \]

A solid cylinder \( x^2+y^2\le1 \), \( 0\le z\le2 \) has density \( \delta(x,y,z)=z \). Find its mass.

Solution: Mass \( =\iiint_E\delta\,dV \), and cylindrical symmetry makes \( r,\theta,z \) natural:

\[ M=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2 z\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=(2\pi)\Big(\frac12\Big)(2)=2\pi. \]

question.en: Practice: Convert the point \( (x,y,z)=(1,1,\sqrt2) \) to spherical coordinates.
